comparison.label: Untrained Inkling 2 Small, free to reason

offshelf_reading.direct: Told to answer at once, 9 of the 19 models did, in the sense that fewer than a quarter of their answers ran past the 512-token limit. Of those, the 4 open-weights models repair 2.3% to 8.0%; the trained Inkling 2 Small repairs 79.5% in about 40 tokens. GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol do better (90.9% to 96.6%) in about 139 to 195 tokens; the other 3 closed models repair 0.0% to 62.5%. Grok 4.7 repairs 98.9% after about 11,278 tokens of reasoning, which its API does not count against the limit.
offshelf_reading.stuck: The other 9 models kept reasoning and were cut off on 53% to 100% of networks. Their figure in that column (0.0% to 43.2%) says how often their reasoning fits in 512 tokens, not how well they answer at a glance: Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Fable 5.2, for example, repair 97% to 100% of the faulty networks they finish.
offshelf_reading.tldr_reason: given 20,000 tokens to reason, Muse Spark Open matches the trained model at about 200 times the tokens
offshelf_reading.reasoning: Free to reason, the 20,000-token limit decides most rows: every model repairs 90% to 100% of the faulty networks it finishes. Muse Spark Open (84.1%) finishes 91% of networks and is level with the trained model, at about 200 times the tokens. The other 7 open models finish 32% to 62% and repair 28.4% to 60.2%. Untrained Inkling 2 Small, at the low reasoning effort used for it throughout, finishes 78% and repairs 77.3%; the 4 closed models finish 96% to 100% and repair 96.6% to 100.0%.
offshelf_reading.paired: Paired on the same 88 faulty networks, among the models that answered at once: GPT-6 Astra (+17.0 points [+8.0, +26.1]) and GPT-6.1 Sol (+11.4 points [+2.3, +21.6]) are ahead of the trained Inkling 2 Small, and the other 7 are behind it (the closest, Gemini 4 Carbon, by 17.0 points [4.5, 29.5]).
offshelf_reading.method: Each model was given the first 100 networks of the in-distribution test set (88 of them faulty) through OpenRouter, with the same two prompts as Inkling 2 Small: told to answer at once (the lowest reasoning setting its API accepts, 512-token limit), then free to reason (20,000-token limit).
offshelf_reading.note: An answer cut off at the limit counts as not repaired, for every model including Inkling 2 Small; "cut off" is the share of the 100 networks where that happened. Tokens are the mean generated per network, reasoning included. The limits were chosen for Inkling 2 Small (512 tokens is ample for an answer, and its own limit there is 256; 20,000 is where its reasoning mostly finishes at the effort used), and the other models reasoned at their provider's default effort, so the with-reasoning column compares models at a fixed budget, not at their best. \* Added after the first results, answer-at-once only. Two with-reasoning runs were left out for cost, before either had produced an answer.

example.prompt:
You are debugging a small ReLU network by reading its weights. The network was built to implement the specification below. It either works correctly or contains exactly one fault (for example a corrupted, mis-scaled, sign-flipped, shifted or swapped part of one tensor). Some neurons are legitimately redundant or inactive; those are not faults.

## Specification
Inputs: 3 inputs x0..x2, each an integer from 0 to 9.
Target: Output max(x1 - x0, 0) + 6.
Outputs: 1 output(s). An output counts as correct when it is within 0.5 of the target value.

## Architecture
h1 = relu(W1 @ x + b1)  [3 neurons]
y = W2 @ h1 + b2  [1 output, no relu]

## Weights
W1 (3 rows x 3 cols) and b1. Row i = incoming weights of h1[i]; column j = outgoing weights of x[j].
  W1[0] = [1.71, -1.71, -1.71]   b1[0] = 3.41
  W1[1] = [-1.31, 1.31, 0]   b1[1] = 0
  W1[2] = [1.95, -1.95, -1.95]   b1[2] = 3.91
W2 (1 rows x 3 cols) and b2. Row i = incoming weights of y[i]; column j = outgoing weights of h1[j].
  W2[0] = [-0.51, 0.76, 0.58]   b2[0] = 6.01

## Your task
Reply with a JSON list of at most 3 edit operations that repairs the network, or [] if it has no fault. Each operation changes one row, one column or one scalar. Indices are 0-based. Allowed operations (examples):
{"op": "scale", "tensor": "W2", "axis": "col", "index": 4, "factor": -1}   multiply one row or column of a weight matrix
{"op": "swap", "tensor": "W2", "axis": "col", "i": 1, "j": 5}   swap two rows or two columns of a weight matrix
{"op": "set", "tensor": "W1", "index": [3, 0], "value": 0.5}   overwrite one weight (index is [row, col])
{"op": "set", "tensor": "b1", "index": 3, "value": -1.5}   overwrite one bias
{"op": "add", "tensor": "W2", "axis": "col", "index": 2, "vector": [0.5, -0.5]}   add a vector to one row or column
{"op": "swap", "tensor": "b2", "i": 0, "j": 2}   swap two biases (scale and add also work on a bias: use "index" with "factor" or "value")
Your edit is scored only by how the edited network behaves on held-out inputs, so any edit that restores the specified behaviour is accepted. Editing a network that has no fault is penalised, and so is an invalid or over-budget answer. End your reply with the JSON list and nothing after it. Answer immediately from your reading of the weights: output only the JSON list, with no reasoning, no calculations and no explanation.

caveats: The edit removes one habit; it does not add math ability. Banning the "Wait" token, with no weight change, scores 38.8%.
One model and one known failure, and every edit in the table is in layer 23. In layer 22 the same proposers gave the same kind of edit and 1 of 16 helped.
We chose the slice the proposer sees, and its prompt names the failure. Finding one neuron among 86,016 from raw weights, as the published runs did, is a harder search.
GPT-6 Astra's edit in Takehi et al., found with 50 forward passes, reaches 48.1%.
qwen.summary: Qwen3.5-0.8B gets stuck repeating lines that start with "Wait" and runs out of tokens: it solves 8.2% of MATH-500. We showed Inkling 2 Small one MLP layer of Qwen as a small table read from its weights, six tokens by 64 neurons, and wrote its answer into the real model. Scaling down how hard layer 23 pushes the two "Wait" tokens lifts MATH-500 to 38.2% [34.0, 42.4], level with the published one-neuron edit that was found with closed frontier models (+1.2 points [-3.0, +5.4] on the 500 problems both were run on). Untrained Inkling 2 Small proposed that edit, reasoning for about 1,685 tokens per answer. Proposers trained by RL on Tinker, on small networks only, give the same kind of edit in one answer of about 137 tokens with no reasoning.
qwen.across: Random edits to the same table do as well. By the comparison fixed before any edit was scored (each proposer's best edit per layer for layers 16-23, on 256 practice problems), random edits gain 10.3 points on average, against 6.9 to 7.7 for Inkling 2 Small with reasoning and the two RL proposers, and 1.9 for the final repair model. In layer 23 the RL proposers do stand out (15 of their 16 answers helped, against 2 of 8 random edits), but the table has only six rows and 20 of the 61 random whole-row edits helped, so much of this result comes from the table we chose to show. The best random edit (swapping the " So" and " Wait" rows in layer 23) scores 36.7% on the practice problems, against 39.1% to 43.0% for the edits in the table below.

fields.offshelf_direct: Told to answer at once, 9 of the 19 models did, in the sense that fewer than a quarter of their answers ran past the 512-token limit. Of those, the 4 open-weights models repair 2.3% to 8.0%; the trained Inkling 2 Small repairs 79.5% in about 40 tokens. GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol do better (90.9% to 96.6%) in about 139 to 195 tokens; the other 3 closed models repair 0.0% to 62.5%. Grok 4.7 repairs 98.9% after about 11,278 tokens of reasoning, which its API does not count against the limit.
fields.offshelf_stuck: The other 9 models kept reasoning and were cut off on 53% to 100% of networks. Their figure in that column (0.0% to 43.2%) says how often their reasoning fits in 512 tokens, not how well they answer at a glance: Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Fable 5.2, for example, repair 97% to 100% of the faulty networks they finish.
fields.offshelf_reasoning: Free to reason, the 20,000-token limit decides most rows: every model repairs 90% to 100% of the faulty networks it finishes. Muse Spark Open (84.1%) finishes 91% of networks and is level with the trained model, at about 200 times the tokens. The other 7 open models finish 32% to 62% and repair 28.4% to 60.2%. Untrained Inkling 2 Small, at the low reasoning effort used for it throughout, finishes 78% and repairs 77.3%; the 4 closed models finish 96% to 100% and repair 96.6% to 100.0%.
fields.offshelf_lead: Each model was given the first 100 networks of the in-distribution test set (88 of them faulty) through OpenRouter, with the same two prompts as Inkling 2 Small: told to answer at once (the lowest reasoning setting its API accepts, 512-token limit), then free to reason (20,000-token limit).
fields.offshelf_note: An answer cut off at the limit counts as not repaired, for every model including Inkling 2 Small; "cut off" is the share of the 100 networks where that happened. Tokens are the mean generated per network, reasoning included. The limits were chosen for Inkling 2 Small (512 tokens is ample for an answer, and its own limit there is 256; 20,000 is where its reasoning mostly finishes at the effort used), and the other models reasoned at their provider's default effort, so the with-reasoning column compares models at a fixed budget, not at their best. * Added after the first results, answer-at-once only. Two with-reasoning runs were left out for cost, before either had produced an answer.
fields.offshelf_tldr_reason: ; given 20,000 tokens to reason, Muse Spark Open matches the trained model at about 200 times the tokens
fields.limits_llm: On the real LLM, random edits to the same table did as well as the proposers; the edit that works is in one layer of one model and removes one known failure rather than adding ability.
